entries.answer: A thesis statement is a single sentence naming what the essay argues, and it belongs in the introduction where the reader can find it in one pass. Its job is to be falsifiable: if no evidence could count against it, it is a description rather than an argument. The common failure is a topic sentence instead, and I will discuss the causes of the war is the shape of it, since it could be argued about indefinitely without saying which way.

patterns: how long should a paragraph be
entries.answer: A paragraph is a unit with one controlling idea, and its job is to develop that idea rather than to introduce a new one. The topic sentence carries the claim and the rest of the paragraph supplies reasons, evidence or steps, and a paragraph that changes claim halfway has two paragraphs' worth of work at neither one's depth. This is why the middle of an essay is usually a list of things, and the fix is to write one sentence per paragraph first and check that they are not duplicates.

entries.answer: A draft is a complete version written to be improved rather than to be right, and the reason it feels wrong to write is that it is being judged while it is being made. The rule is to finish before editing, because editing a half-finished draft produces a tidier half-finished draft. Time is the real constraint: a draft written quickly and then cut is faster than a draft polished sentence by sentence, and it is also easier to cut a finished thing than to imagine a finished thing.

patterns: do I need to cite a common fact
entries.answer: A citation credits the source of an idea, a quotation or a figure, and there are two systems with different logic. Author-date citation credits the person, while numbered citation credits the position in a list, and the second is more compact when there are many references. What a citation is not is a decoration added at the end, since a source cited but not discussed, or discussed but not cited, are the two most common faults and only one of them looks like an error.

entries.answer: Plagiarism is presenting somebody else's work as your own, and the definition is stricter than most people expect, covering sentences, ideas and structure. Direct copying is the obvious case, but the ones that catch people out are paraphrasing with inadequate attribution and reusing your own earlier work without saying so, which is self-plagiarism. The reliable defence is not wording but provenance: write from a source while it is open, so the ideas arrive in your own structure, and record where each came from.
